common_name: Elijah Blue Fescue (Compact Intense-Blue Ornamental Grass)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall in very well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Elijah Blue is the most widely sold blue fescue cultivar, selected for a more compact habit and more intense, consistent blue color than the straight species.

directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, lean to average soil; Elijah Blue is the standard nursery-trade blue fescue cultivar, selected for tight, uniform, intensely silvery-blue mounds of needle-fine foliage that hold their color and neat habit more reliably than seed-grown plants of the straight species. It is a cool-season grass that grows most vigorously in spring and fall and can go semi-dormant or look ragged during the peak heat and humidity of a Gulf Coast summer, so give it the best possible drainage and avoid heavy, wet clay, which promotes crown rot far faster than drought stress does. Slender tan flower spikes rise just above the foliage in early summer. Divide clumps every two to three years in early spring, discarding the woody, browned-out center and replanting the vigorous outer sections, which keeps the blue color and tight mounding habit at its best. Excellent as edging, in rock gardens, or massed as a low, textural groundcover in a sunny, well-drained bed.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun; giant reed spreads aggressively by rhizome and is classified as invasive in many warm, wet regions including parts of the Gulf South — confine roots with a barrier or avoid planting near streams, ditches, or natural areas where it can escape into waterways.

directions: Plant in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun, ideally in a large, contained bed with a sturdy root barrier; giant reed is an enormous, bamboo-like ornamental grass capable of reaching 15–20 feet in a single season, historically valued for fast, dense screening, windbreaks, and erosion control on slopes and streambanks, with broad, blue-green, cane-like foliage and tall, plume-like flower heads in late summer and fall. Its extraordinary vigor is also its major drawback: giant reed spreads aggressively by thick underground rhizomes and readily escapes cultivation into wet ditches, streams, and floodplains across the warmer, wetter parts of the country, where it is classified as invasive and actively removed by land managers because it crowds out native riparian vegetation and increases wildfire fuel load when dry. Because of this, site it only where root spread can be fully contained — a large in-ground barrier, a bed surrounded by pavement, or a large container — and never plant it near natural waterways, wetlands, or unmanaged land. Cut old canes to the ground in late winter before new growth begins to keep plantings tidy.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Assessment of Non-Native Plants

common_name: Graziella Miniature Maiden Grass (Narrow Early-Flowering Miscanthus)

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; Graziella is a compact, narrow-bladed maiden grass cultivar selected for earlier flowering than many other Miscanthus sinensis cultivars, giving reliable plume display even in shorter-season gardens.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; Graziella is a refined, narrow-leaved maiden grass cultivar valued for its tidy, upright, vase-shaped habit and notably early flowering compared to many other Miscanthus sinensis selections, sending up silvery-pink plumes by late summer that mature to a warm, silvery-tan and persist attractively through much of winter, adding movement and structure to the garden even in the dormant season. The fine, arching, dark-green foliage turns attractive gold and copper tones in fall before going dormant. Because it flowers earlier and reliably in a wide range of climates, it is a dependable choice where a longer, cooler growing season limits bloom on later-flowering miscanthus cultivars. Cut the entire clump back to a few inches above the ground in late winter before new growth emerges, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor and a tidy, upright form.

common_name: Fireworks Fountain Grass (Variegated Pink-Burgundy Ornamental Grass)

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants after last frost in full sun and very well-drained soil; this cultivar does not come true from seed and is propagated by division. Fireworks is more strikingly variegated but generally less vigorous than plain purple fountain grass.

directions: Plant after last frost in full sun and very well-drained soil; Fireworks fountain grass is a striking variegated cultivar with slender, arching blades striped in hot pink, burgundy, and creamy white over a dark red-purple base — considerably showier and more colorful than plain purple fountain grass ('Rubrum'), making it a strong accent or container centerpiece plant through the heat of summer. It thrives in full sun and dry-to-average soil once established, tolerating heat and drought well but requiring consistent moisture during the first few weeks after transplanting. Like other Pennisetum setaceum selections it is grown as a warm-season annual outside of zone 9–11, or can be overwintered as a houseplant in a bright spot after cutting back before the first frost. In frost-free climates it can persist as a short-lived perennial and self-seed; remove spent flower plumes before seed set if naturalizing is a concern in warmer zones. Divide congested clumps in spring if grown as a perennial.

common_name: Pumila Dwarf Pampas Grass (Compact Ornamental Plume Grass)

planting.note: Plant container divisions after last frost in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Pumila is a compact cultivar of pampas grass, reaching roughly a third the size of the straight species, making it more manageable for a smaller residential garden.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Pumila is a compact selection of pampas grass, reaching only about 4–6 feet in bloom compared to the 8–10-plus feet of the straight species, which makes it far more practical for a standard residential landscape while retaining the same dramatic, silvery-white plumes held well above the arching, fine-textured foliage from late summer into fall. It is a tough, drought-tolerant grass once established, tolerating heat, wind, and poor soil with ease, and works well as a specimen, screen, or accent at a scale that overwhelms most gardens when the full-sized species is used instead. The narrow leaf blades have sharp, saw-toothed edges, so wear gloves and long sleeves when cutting the clump back hard in late winter before new growth begins. Because pampas grass can self-seed and naturalize in some regions, deadhead spent plumes before seed drop if planting near natural areas, and confirm local guidance, since it is considered invasive in parts of the Gulf South and West Coast.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown rosettes in spring in very well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun; unlike hens-and-chicks, Jovibarba rosettes multiply by splitting the crown into new rosettes ('rollers') rather than by sending out offsets on runners.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, gritty to sandy soil in full sun; Jovibarba is a close relative of Sempervivum (hens-and-chicks) commonly sold alongside it for rock gardens, troughs, and xeriscape plantings, but it multiplies in a genuinely different way — instead of producing new rosettes on runners like Sempervivum, mature Jovibarba rosettes split at the crown into several new rosettes, which loosen and can simply roll away from the mother plant to root nearby, giving rise to the common name 'rollers.' Rosettes are typically green to bronze, sometimes with reddish tips in strong sun, and form tight, low mats that spread slowly to cover gravel beds, rock crevices, and shallow containers. It is extremely drought-tolerant and cold-hardy once established, needing excellent drainage above all else — soggy soil, not cold, is what kills it. Like Sempervivum, individual rosettes are monocarpic, flowering once on a tall stalk and then dying, but the surrounding offsets carry the planting on indefinitely. Ideal for rock gardens, green roofs, and any lean, sharply drained, sunny spot where little else will thrive.
